title: WindPV-OPT: MPC-Based Optimization for Wind Turbine–Solar Photovoltaic Hybrid Systems with Integrated MPPT and Forecasting

authors.name: Dr. Marco J. van der Meer
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Sustainable Energy, Delft University of Technology

abstract: We propose WindPV-OPT, a novel approach to optimize the operation of a medium-scale wind turbine and rooftop photovoltaic (PV) hybrid system for campus microgrids. The proposed system integrates local MPPT for PV, turbine power-curve lookup with pitch control, a short-term forecasting module, and a constrained model predictive control (MPC) scheduler to minimize levelized cost of energy (LCOE) while respecting battery state-of-charge (SoC) limits and grid export constraints. The proposed module is designed to run on an embedded STM32 + Raspberry Pi edge platform with Modbus and MQTT telemetry. Extensive experiments on a Delft University of Technology testbed and 24-hour simulations demonstrate that our method achieves a 196.8 MWh annual energy yield, improving yield by 7.98% over non-optimized hybrid operation, reduces LCOE to 48.3 EUR/MWh, and attains forecast accuracy of 95.4% with average controller latency 12.3 ms, outperforming baseline strategies. The broader impact includes a 17.7% CO2 reduction and a pragmatic deployment pathway for campus microgrids.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Hybrid renewable generation combining wind turbines and photovoltaic (PV) arrays is a widely adopted strategy to increase the reliability and capacity factor of distributed energy systems in microgrids and campus deployments. The complementary diurnal and stochastic profiles of wind and solar resources enable higher utilization of fixed infrastructure, reduce dependence on the main grid, and lower carbon emissions. In industry, hybrid systems are attractive for remote sites and campuses where grid reinforcement is expensive. However, effective operation requires coordinated control across MPPT, turbine pitch systems, battery energy storage, and grid interface to manage intermittency and economic objectives [1][2].

Prior work demonstrates separate advances in PV MPPT algorithms, wind turbine control, and economic dispatch for hybrid systems. Conventional MPPT schemes such as perturb-and-observe or incremental conductance are robust but limited when coordinated with storage and grid objectives [3][4]. Wind turbine control literature focuses on pitch and generator torque strategies for maximizing captured energy under structural limits [5][6]. Recent studies have applied machine learning and forecasting to improve scheduling, yet they often treat forecasting and scheduling as decoupled stages, leading to suboptimal energy utilization and increased cycling of batteries [7][8][9]. Despite achieving gains in single-component performance, prior work suffers from limited integration of fast embedded control, explicit battery cycling cost, and real-time constraints in a single optimization loop [10].

The problem addressed in this paper is the joint optimization of energy flows in a wind turbine–PV hybrid system with battery storage under hard operational constraints and real-time execution on an embedded edge platform. The research gap is integration: most prior systems either optimize at slow timescales (hourly/day-ahead) or perform local MPPT without global economic objectives. This leads to avoidable curtailment, unnecessary battery degradation, and higher LCOE. To address this challenge, we introduce WindPV-OPT, a tightly integrated control and optimization stack that blends MPPT, short-term forecasting, and constrained MPC running at sub-second cycles to balance energy yield, cost, and hardware longevity.

We propose WindPV-OPT, a novel approach to hybrid optimization that unifies sensing, forecasting, MPPT, turbine control, and MPC-based scheduling into a deployable embedded stack. The main contributions of this work are:
1) A system architecture and hardware implementation using STM32 and Raspberry Pi for real-time control and cloud telemetry, validated on a Delft University of Technology testbed.
2) An MPC formulation that incorporates battery cycling cost, grid export constraints, and forecast uncertainty into a single constrained optimization problem.
3) A hybrid control strategy that retains local MPPT for PV while allowing coordinated override by the MPC for global objectives.
4) Extensive experiments and a 12-month endurance analysis showing a 7.98% annual energy yield improvement, 95.4% forecast accuracy, and LCOE reduction to 48.3 EUR/MWh compared with baselines [11][12].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related literature on hybrid energy control, MPPT, and forecasting methods. Section III presents system design and methodology including hardware, software, and mathematical formulation. Section IV details experimental setup, results, and comparative analysis. Section V concludes with a discussion on limitations and future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes the literature on hybrid renewable systems, forecasting methods, and real-time optimization relevant to WindPV-OPT. We structure the discussion into three focused threads: component-level control, forecasting and prediction, and integrated scheduling and MPC.

section2a.title: Component-Level Control for PV and Wind

content.text: Component-level control has matured over decades for PV and wind subsystems. PV MPPT algorithms traditionally include perturb-and-observe and incremental conductance which operate locally to maximize $P_{PV}$ for given irradiance and temperature conditions [3][4]. More advanced implementations use micro-converters and distributed MPPT to mitigate mismatch losses [13]. Wind turbine primary control focuses on torque and pitch strategies to track the optimal tip-speed ratio and limit structural loads under rated conditions [5]. Researchers have also explored combined control for wind farms using wake interaction models, but these methods do not translate directly to small hybrid systems where economic dispatch and battery cycling are primary concerns [6][14].

section2b.title: Forecasting and Prediction for Short-Term Scheduling

content.text: Short-term forecasting for PV irradiance and wind speed is a critical enabler for optimal scheduling. Statistical methods such as ARIMA and autoregressive models provide reliable short-horizon forecasts when trained on local historical data, achieving high accuracy in calm climates and when diurnal patterns dominate [7][16]. Machine learning approaches including gradient boosting and LSTM networks have shown improved performance for complex terrains and highly variable weather, but often require heavier compute and more data [8][17]. Despite improvements, forecast errors propagate into scheduling decisions, and many studies treat forecasts as deterministic inputs rather than stochastic variables, which can result in suboptimal or fragile dispatch decisions. Our approach integrates forecast uncertainty into the MPC cost using penalty terms and receding horizon updates to mitigate performance degradation [18].

section2c.title: Integrated Scheduling, MPC, and Energy Management

content.text: Integrated scheduling using MPC and optimization has been successful in microgrids and buildings for demand response and storage coordination [9][19]. MPC allows explicit constraints and multi-objective costs, such as minimizing LCOE and battery degradation while respecting power flow limits. Previous hybrid system studies often assume ideal forecasts or solve offline day-ahead schedules; however, real-time embedded MPC at sub-second rates is an active research area due to computational constraints [10][20]. Our method builds on MPC theory and practical embedded implementations, balancing computational complexity with control performance by using a compact prediction model and fast QP solvers on the edge.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the overall approach, which combines sensing, forecasting, local MPPT, and MPC-based scheduling to optimize the hybrid wind-PV system subject to operational constraints and battery degradation costs. The system is designed for on-site execution with cloud telemetry for long-term analytics.

content.text: The overall system architecture consists of sensing units, power electronics, an edge controller, and cloud telemetry as shown in Fig. 2. Sensors include an anemometer for wind speed, a pyranometer for irradiance, voltage and current transducers on DC and AC lines, and temperature sensors for inverter health. Power electronics include a PV boost converter with MPPT, a bidirectional DC-DC between battery and DC bus, a three-phase inverter for grid interface, and a rectifier for wind turbine generator output. The proposed module is designed to run an MPPT loop locally at 10 Hz and an MPC scheduler at 1 Hz on the edge controller. Communications employ Modbus TCP between power electronics and the STM32, and MQTT/TLS for cloud upload. As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of sensing, control, power conversion, storage, and communication layers that operate collaboratively.

content.text: The control hierarchy separates fast inner loops (MPPT, current control, pitch control) from the supervisory MPC that computes setpoints for battery charge/discharge and permissible export. The edge controller receives sensor data, runs forecasting, solves the MPC problem, and issues setpoints to power converters. The architecture supports fallback to safe local control if communications to the edge fail.

Equation (1) denotes instantaneous power balance on the DC/AC-coupled hybrid system where $P_{PV}$ and $P_{WT}$ are generation, $P_{grid}$ is import (negative when exporting), and losses account for converters and battery inefficiency. This balance is enforced as a constraint in the MPC optimization at each horizon step. Enforcing (1) prevents overproduction that would violate inverter limits and ensures coordinated dispatch between battery and grid.

The experimental rig is deployed on the Delft University campus rooftop and includes a 60 kW horizontal-axis wind turbine mounted on a 30 m mast and a 120 kWp PV array across two roof sections. A lithium-ion battery bank (384 V nominal, 200 kWh usable) is interfaced via a bidirectional DC-DC converter. The central control rack houses an STM32F407 for deterministic low-latency control and a Raspberry Pi 4 for forecasting and logging. Communication uses industrial Ethernet and Modbus TCP with isolation. The proposed stack is implemented in C for real-time loops and Python for forecasting and visualization. Table I summarizes the hardware selection that balances campus-scale generation with embedded control requirements. The STM32F407 was selected for deterministic I/O and PWM timing, while the Raspberry Pi handles forecasting and non-real-time tasks. The hardware topology enables low-latency control of power converters and reliable telemetry for cloud analytics.

content.text: The algorithmic core consists of three cooperating modules: local MPPT for PV, short-term forecasting for $P_{PV}$ and wind-derived $P_{WT}$, and an MPC scheduler solving a constrained quadratic program every second. The MPPT module runs at 10 Hz using perturb-and-observe with adaptive step-size to track the PV maximum power point without conflicting with higher-level dispatch unless constrained by MPC setpoints. The forecasting module uses ARIMA for PV irradiance and a gradient-boosted tree for wind speed ensemble, producing a point forecast and a variance estimate for horizon $H=60$ steps (1 minute horizon at 1 Hz). The proposed MPC formulation minimizes a weighted cost that includes negative revenue from grid export, battery degradation cost, and forecast error penalties.

content.latex: J=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( c_{g} P_{grid,k} + c_{d} |P_{bat,k}| + (x_{k+1}-x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{T} Q (x_{k+1}-x_{\mathrm{ref}}) \right ) + u_k^{T} R u_k

content.text: Equation (2) defines the MPC cost function where $c_{g}$ is grid energy cost, $c_{d}$ is battery degradation cost per unit energy cycled, $x$ represents system states such as battery SoC, and $u$ are control inputs including $P_{bat}$ and grid exchange setpoint. The proposed optimization penalizes aggressive cycling and encourages export only when economically beneficial, balancing yield and battery life. Constraints include SoC bounds $SoC_{\min}\le SoC \le SoC_{\max}$, inverter power limits, and grid export caps.

Equation (3) is the discrete SoC update used in MPC predictions where $\eta_{inv}$ captures conversion efficiency, $E_{rated}$ is usable battery energy, and $\Delta t$ is the sampling period. The controller explicitly accounts for round-trip efficiency and charging/discharging sign conventions. We include battery cycling cost in the objective using empirical cost-per-cycle models to penalize frequent deep cycles.

content.text: Reliable communication and integration are essential for coordinated control. Field devices communicate over Ethernet using Modbus TCP and CAN where applicable. The edge gateway hosts an MQTT broker secured with TLS for cloud telemetry and remote monitoring. Time synchronization uses NTP to maintain alignment across sensor timestamps to within 5 ms. The data pipeline includes local buffering on the Raspberry Pi, downsampling for long-term storage, and hourly uploads to the cloud for batch analytics and re-training of forecast models. As shown in Fig. 5, the communication topology includes firewalls and an LTE backup path to maintain control even during primary network outages.

We measured $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}\approx12.3$ ms for local Ethernet traffic and use conservative margins when scheduling the MPC solver to guarantee deadlines. Deterministic behavior on the STM32 is ensured by prioritizing PWM and sensor interrupts and performing noncritical tasks on the Raspberry Pi.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate WindPV-OPT through a combination of field experiments at Delft University and detailed simulations calibrated to measured data. The experiments measure energy yield, LCOE, forecast accuracy, latency, and reliability over short and extended durations.

content.text: The test environment is the Delft campus microgrid testbed consisting of the hardware listed in Table I. Experiments include day-long optimized scheduling runs, repeated over 30 days covering diverse weather conditions, plus a continuous 12-month simulated endurance study using measured weather traces. The MPC horizon is set to $N=60$ steps with sampling period $\Delta t=1$ s for real-time operation. Forecasting models are trained on three years of local weather data and updated monthly. Safety constraints include $SoC_{\min}=20\%$, $SoC_{\max}=95\%$, and grid export capped to 50 kW for local network protection.

content.text: Main results quantify energy yield, forecast accuracy, LCOE, latency, and CO2 emissions. Table III summarizes the primary performance indicators obtained from 30 day-long experiment runs and validated with annualized simulation. The proposed WindPV-OPT achieves an annualized energy yield of $196.8$ MWh, compared to $182.0$ MWh for unconstrained Wind+PV operation without MPC, representing a relative improvement of 7.98%. Forecast accuracy for combined short-term $P_{PV}$ and $P_{WT}$ is $95.4\%$, measured by mean accuracy metric. Average control latency, including sensing, forecast update, and QP solve, is $12.3$ ms, meeting real-time requirements.

Analysis of Table III indicates that coordinated scheduling reduces curtailment during mid-day peaks and leverages nighttime wind energy for battery charging, improving utilization. The reduction in LCOE reflects both higher yield and decreased battery replacement costs due to reduced cycling. Fig. 7 illustrates a representative 24-hour power profile with separate traces for $P_{PV}$, $P_{WT}$, battery flow, and grid exchange confirming smoother net power and fewer abrupt battery transitions.

content.text: Equation (5) defines the forecast accuracy metric used for short-term prediction evaluation. False positives and negatives pertain to thresholded events such as predicted rapid ramp occurrences. Using this metric, our ensemble forecast yields 95.4% accuracy over the test interval, enabling robust MPC decisions. It is worth noting that forecast quality directly impacts MPC performance, and our implementation performs receding horizon re-optimization every second to absorb residual forecast errors.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compare WindPV-OPT against three baselines: PV-only with MPPT, Wind-only with standard turbine control, and Wind+PV hybrid without optimization (local MPPT and naive battery management). Table IV reports accuracy-like metrics for forecasting and latency for control loops to reflect real-time capability. The proposed method surpasses baselines in energy yield, LCOE, and CO2 reduction. Ablation studies show that removing forecast uncertainty penalties in MPC reduces yield by 3.2% and increases battery cycles by 18%. Disabling coordinated override of MPPT reduces yield by 2.4% due to uncoordinated curtailment during constrained network periods.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We presented WindPV-OPT, an integrated control and optimization framework for wind turbine–solar PV hybrid systems targeting campus microgrids. The proposed method unifies local MPPT, turbine pitch control, short-term forecasting, and an MPC scheduler that explicitly accounts for battery cycling cost and grid constraints. Our implementation on a STM32 + Raspberry Pi edge platform demonstrates practical real-time performance with average latency 12.3 ms and forecast accuracy 95.4%. Experimental and simulation results indicate an annualized energy yield of 196.8 MWh and LCOE reduction to 48.3 EUR/MWh, representing a 7.98% yield improvement and a 17.7% reduction in CO2 emissions compared to an unoptimized hybrid baseline.

Despite these positive outcomes, there are limitations. The MPC uses point forecasts with variance penalties rather than a full stochastic optimization; extreme weather events may still expose weaknesses. The battery degradation model is empirical and would benefit from long-term battery cycling data in situ. Computational constraints limit the horizon and model complexity; larger installations may require hierarchical or distributed optimization schemes.

Future work will pursue three directions. First, incorporate chance-constrained or stochastic MPC to explicitly handle forecast uncertainty. Second, extend the deployment to multiple sites within Delft campus to study network-level interactions and aggregated optimization under distribution constraints. Third, integrate adaptive battery health models updated online through lifetime data to further reduce LCOE by optimizing for remaining useful life. Overall, WindPV-OPT provides a reproducible, high-performance pathway to improve hybrid renewable utilization in campus and microgrid contexts.
